questions.question: The surah opens by describing the Prophet Muhammad as Allah's 'Abd (servant). What does the tafsir identify as the significance of this title in this opening verse?
options: A. It emphasizes that the Prophet was an ordinary human with no special qualities
B. It is the highest honorific given to the Prophet, reflecting the pinnacle of servitude to Allah
C. It signals that the revelation was sent to comfort the Prophet in worldly distress
D. It refers specifically to the Prophet's role as a political leader of Madinah
questions.explanation: The tafsir explains that calling the Prophet 'Abd (servant) is not a diminishment but the highest honor — complete surrender to Allah is the mark of true greatness. The verse also states there is no 'iwaj (crookedness) in the Book, meaning it is perfectly straight and balanced.

questions.question: True or False: Classical scholars reached a clear consensus on the meaning of 'al-Raqim' mentioned alongside the People of the Cave, identifying it definitively as the name of a tablet bearing the youths' names.
questions.explanation: Imam al-Tabari recorded multiple competing opinions on al-Raqim — including that it was a tablet, a valley, a mountain, or the name of the village — and did not settle on one definitive meaning. The word thus remained a matter of scholarly debate rather than consensus.

questions.question: Verse 7 describes everything on earth as 'zinah' (adornment) created to test which people excel in deeds. Which contemporary Sunni scholar stressed that this verse establishes a comprehensive framework linking worldly beauty to moral accountability?
options: A. Sayyid Qutb, who read the verse as a condemnation of all material possessions
B. Wahbah al-Zuhayli, who explained that the world's adornment is purposeful and divinely designed as a test of 'ahsan amal' (best deeds)
C. Ibn Uthaymeen, who argued that 'zinah' refers only to wealth and children
D. Muhammad al-Sha'rawi, who interpreted 'zinah' as restricted to the natural landscape
questions.explanation: Wahbah al-Zuhayli in al-Tafsir al-Munir emphasized that 'zinah' encompasses all earthly attractions and that their creation has a divine purpose: to test which human beings will prioritize righteous deeds ('ahsan amal') over indulging in worldly allure.

questions.question: When the young men fled to the cave, verse 10 records their supplication asking Allah for two specific gifts. What were those two gifts?
options: A. Provision (rizq) and a long life
B. Mercy (rahma) from Allah and guidance (rashad) in their affair
C. Victory over their people and a safe return to the city
D. Knowledge ('ilm) and a clear sign to prove their faith
questions.explanation: The youths' prayer in verse 10 — 'Rabbana atina min ladunka rahmatan wa hayyi' lana min amrina rashada' — asked specifically for divine mercy (rahma) and sound guidance (rashad). This balanced request shows their complete reliance on Allah rather than on any worldly plan.

questions.question: True or False: Ibn Kathir used verse 13's statement that the youths' guidance was increased ('wa zidnahum hudan') as evidence for the Sunni position that iman (faith) can increase and decrease.
questions.explanation: Ibn Kathir in his Tafsir cited verse 13 — 'wa zidnahum hudan' — as a Quranic proof for the Sunni 'aqida that faith is not static but increases with acts of obedience and decreases through sin. The youths' courageous stand before the king was itself a deed that increased their guidance.

questions.question: Verse 17 describes how the sun's path moves away from the cave's opening at rising and setting. What protective function does the tafsir assign to this divinely arranged phenomenon?
options: A. It allowed sunlight to dry out the cave so disease could not grow
B. It ensured the sleepers were not disturbed by heat or light, preserving their miraculous sleep
C. It marked the direction of qibla for the youths when they prayed
D. It signaled the exact number of years they would sleep
questions.explanation: The tafsir explains that Allah arranged the sun's angle so it passed over the cave's entrance without penetrating directly inside, protecting the sleepers from harsh heat and light. This was part of the miracle: the physical environment was divinely managed to preserve them. The verse then concludes that guidance belongs to Allah alone.

questions.question: True or False: Ibn Abbas, as recorded by Imam al-Tabari, stated that the youths' sides were turned twice each day throughout their sleep in the cave.
questions.explanation: According to Ibn Abbas as transmitted by Imam al-Tabari, the youths were turned twice each year — once toward the south and once toward the north — not twice per day. This turning was a miraculous act to prevent their bodies from decomposing or developing sores during their long supernatural sleep.

questions.question: True or False: The tafsir identifies the parable of the two gardens in verses 32-44 as being directed specifically at the proud chiefs of Quraysh who mocked the poor Muslim companions of the Prophet.
questions.explanation: The tafsir explains that the parable of the two men with gardens was revealed in the context of Quraysh leaders who scorned the socially humble believers around the Prophet. The story of the arrogant garden-owner served as a direct warning to those leaders about the danger of pride and ingratitude.

questions.question: In verse 35 the arrogant man enters his garden described as 'zalimun li-nafsihi' (wronging himself). How does Sayyid Qutb interpret this self-description in the context of the parable?
options: A. It is an admission of guilt that the man immediately repents from
B. It reveals the man's spiritual blindness — he boasts and denies Allah's power without realizing that this arrogance is itself the deepest form of self-harm
C. It indicates that the man was wronging himself by spending wealth on the garden rather than on charity
D. Sayyid Qutb reads it as divine judgment pronounced on the man from outside, not a self-description
questions.explanation: Sayyid Qutb in Fi Zilal al-Quran noted that 'zalimun li-nafsihi' reveals the man's spiritual blindness: he walks into his garden denying that it could ever perish, not realizing that arrogance and denial of Allah's power is the deepest form of self-harm. The label exposes his condition even as he boasts.

questions.question: In verse 37, the believing companion rebukes the arrogant garden-owner by reminding him of his origin. What argument does the companion use to deflate his pride?
options: A. He warns the owner that his trees will wither without rain from Allah
B. He reminds him that he was created from dust, then a drop of fluid, and then fashioned into a man — humble origins that make arrogance absurd
C. He quotes a previous prophet who lost his wealth because of ingratitude
D. He points out that the garden's produce belongs to the workers, not the owner
questions.explanation: The believing companion's rebuttal in verse 37 grounds the arrogant man by invoking the stages of human creation: from turab (dust) to nutfa (a drop) to a fully formed man. The tafsir highlights this as a classic Quranic argument — one cannot be proud of wealth when one's origin was so humble and entirely dependent on Allah's creative act.

questions.question: Verse 65 introduces Khidr as a servant upon whom Allah bestowed mercy and 'ilm ladunni (knowledge from Himself). What position did classical scholars take on what this special knowledge consisted of?
options: A. It was knowledge of all seven heavens and the divine throne
B. It was prophetic knowledge equal in authority to the Quran
C. It was divinely inspired knowledge of hidden realities and causes that ordinary human perception cannot reach
D. It was mastery of the natural sciences, medicine, and astronomy
questions.explanation: Classical scholars including Imam al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explained 'ilm ladunni as a direct divine gift of knowledge about hidden matters — causes and outcomes concealed from ordinary perception. This is why Khidr could act on realities Musa could not yet see, and it is distinct from prophetic revelation or empirical learning.

questions.question: True or False: Ibn Uthaymeen argued that Musa's self-imposed farewell condition in verse 76 — 'if I ask you about anything after this, do not keep me as a companion' — is a lesson universally applicable to students of knowledge who must learn patience and trust in their teacher's process.
questions.explanation: Ibn Uthaymeen drew a broader lesson from verse 76: a true student of knowledge must control impatience, trust the teacher's process, and recognize the limits of their own understanding. Musa's self-imposed condition of separation upon any further impatience models the discipline required in the student-teacher relationship.

questions.question: True or False: Khidr killed the boy because the boy had already committed a serious crime against his parents, not because of what he might do in the future.
questions.explanation: The tafsir explains that Khidr's action was based on divinely granted foreknowledge: the boy would have grown to burden his believing parents with his kufr and corruption. The act was preventive, rooted in Khidr's 'ilm ladunni about what the boy was destined to become, not a punishment for a crime already committed.

questions.question: Classical scholars explained that the question about Dhul-Qarnayn in verse 83 was put to the Quraysh by a group seeking to test the Prophet. Who prompted the Quraysh to ask this question?
options: A. The Byzantine Roman envoys visiting Makkah at the time
B. The rabbis of the Jews in Madinah, who suggested it as a test of the Prophet's prophethood
C. The Persian traders passing through the Hijaz
D. The leaders of the Ethiopian Christian community
questions.explanation: Ibn Kathir and Imam al-Tabari recorded that the Jewish rabbis of Madinah counseled the Quraysh to ask the Prophet about Dhul-Qarnayn as a test, because knowledge of this figure was known from their scriptures and would reveal whether Muhammad was receiving genuine divine revelation.

questions.question: When the people between the two mountains offered Dhul-Qarnayn payment to build a barrier against Yajuj and Majuj, he refused. How does contemporary tafsir interpret this refusal?
options: A. He refused because he doubted the people's ability to raise sufficient funds
B. He refused because accepting payment would reduce a divinely mandated act of justice into a financial transaction, contradicting his role as a trustee of power
C. He refused because the Quran prohibits rulers from accepting tribute from their subjects
D. He refused to demonstrate his military superiority over the mountain people
questions.explanation: Wahbah al-Zuhayli and other contemporary scholars explain that Dhul-Qarnayn's refusal of payment reflects his understanding of kingship as a divine trust (amanah). His resources were sufficient, and accepting wages would have reduced a divinely mandated act of protecting the vulnerable into a financial transaction.

questions.question: True or False: After completing the barrier, Dhul-Qarnayn declared that it was achieved by his own strength and engineering skill, attributing the achievement to himself.
questions.explanation: Verse 96 records Dhul-Qarnayn saying 'haza rahmatun min rabbi' — this is a mercy from my Lord. The tafsir emphasizes that despite his great power and resources, he immediately attributed the achievement to Allah's mercy, not to his own capabilities. This is held up as a model of how a ruler should acknowledge Allah's grace.

questions.question: Verse 110 states that whoever hopes to meet their Lord should do righteous deeds and not associate anyone in worship. Classical scholars identified two conditions for a deed to be accepted by Allah. What are those two conditions?
options: A. The action must be done publicly and with the support of the community
B. The action must be sincere (done for Allah alone) and correct (following the Prophet's method)
C. The action must be accompanied by charity and performed in a state of ritual purity
D. The action must be done consistently for forty days and witnessed by two Muslims
questions.explanation: Ibn Kathir and classical scholars explained that verse 110 encapsulates the two pillars of accepted deeds: ikhlas (sincerity — done for Allah alone, not for show) and mutaba'a (correctness — conforming to the Prophet's practice). An action lacking either condition is rejected regardless of its external form.

questions.question: True or False: Wahbah al-Zuhayli noted that the youths' careful instruction in verse 19 — to enter the city discreetly and buy the purest food — demonstrates that seeking halal (lawful) means remains obligatory even when a person is in danger.
questions.explanation: Wahbah al-Zuhayli used verse 19 to derive the principle that seeking halal provision is not suspended by danger: the youths were instructed to buy 'azka ta'aman (the purest food) even while hiding their identity. Necessity does not automatically permit abandoning the lawful whenever a halal option remains accessible.

questions.question: Verse 14 states 'We bound/strengthened their hearts' (rabatna ala qulubihim) before the youths made their declaration of tawhid before the king. What does this divine act of binding reveal according to the tafsir?
options: A. That the youths had memorized lengthy prayers that gave them inner strength
B. That physical bravery is a natural human trait that requires no divine assistance
C. That divine steadfastness is a grace from Allah that precedes and enables the believer's bold declaration of faith
D. That the youths had sworn an oath among themselves to stand firm, which Allah then ratified
questions.explanation: The tafsir emphasizes that 'rabatna ala qulubihim' — Allah's binding of their hearts — occurred before their declaration, showing that steadfastness in the face of tyrants is not merely a product of human willpower. Divine thabat (firmness) is a grace given to believers who sincerely turn to Allah, making their stand possible.

questions.question: True or False: Ibn Kathir, when discussing the dispute about building over the sleepers' graves in verse 21, endorsed the construction of a mosque over their site as a way of honoring their memory.
questions.explanation: Ibn Kathir explicitly did not endorse building a mosque over the cave. He cited the established hadith in which the Prophet forbade building over graves and cursed those who do so. Ibn Kathir used verse 21 to warn against this practice, noting that those who proposed the mosque were not following sound guidance.

questions.question: Verse 90 describes a people at the eastern limit of Dhul-Qarnayn's journey who had no shelter (sitr) from the rising sun. How do contemporary Sunni scholars use this detail to characterize Dhul-Qarnayn's rule?
options: A. As evidence that Dhul-Qarnayn's empire extended beyond what any ordinary ruler could reach, proving supernatural power
B. As an example of how Dhul-Qarnayn documented geographical discoveries for future generations
C. As a sign that Dhul-Qarnayn assessed the real humanitarian conditions of his subjects and did not ignore the vulnerable and exposed
D. As proof that the eastern people were being punished by Allah for rejecting faith
questions.explanation: Wahbah al-Zuhayli and other contemporary scholars highlight that the detail of the shelterless people shows Dhul-Qarnayn's leadership style: he surveyed the actual welfare of those at the margins of his domain. This is presented as a model of just, attentive governance, reinforced by verse 91's statement that Allah encompassed all he had in knowledge.

questions.question: Verse 2 describes the Quran as 'qayyiman' — upright and actively overseeing. Which of the following best captures the tafsir's distinction between this term and 'no crookedness' (la 'iwaja) in verse 1?
options: A. 'No crookedness' refers to the Quran's Arabic style, while 'qayyim' refers to its legal rulings
B. 'No crookedness' negates any flaw or deviation in the Quran, while 'qayyim' positively affirms it as an upright, active authority that governs and supersedes all previous scriptures
C. Both terms mean the same thing and are simply two ways of saying the Quran is accurate
D. 'Qayyim' specifically describes the Quran's role in economic justice, while 'no crookedness' describes its theological precision
questions.explanation: The tafsir explains that verse 1's 'la 'iwaja' clears the Quran of any defect, while verse 2's 'qayyiman' adds a positive dimension: the Quran is an active, standing authority that oversees and supersedes all previous scriptures. Wahbah al-Zuhayli noted that qayyim carries the meaning of an upright guardian, not merely a passive text.
